description: My name is Muhammad Ahmad. I live in lahore.
summary:
ASTRA is a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Kids aged 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars base and must balance energy between life support, food, radio and radiation shielding while surviving real NASA solar storms. Every choice has a visible cost, so children learn consequence and trade-off, not memorization.

The game pulls real NASA data: DONKI solar flares and CMEs, OSDR astronaut health studies, APOD, and JPL orbital data for the Earth-Mars communication delay. When live data is unreachable it falls back to real archived 2024 events, always clearly labeled LIVE or ARCHIVED, never invented numbers. A Shield Lab lets kids pick a real flare and watch radiation change as they adjust shielding, linking a game decision to actual space weather. Every mission is replayable with a seeded code so failure teaches rather than punishes.

Built as a single offline-capable HTML/JS app with an engine fully separated from the UI and validated by over 72,000 automated tests, ASTRA is accurate, accessible, and ready for classrooms.
details:
ASTRA is a browser-based simulation game. Each school day (called a “sol”), players allocate limited solar energy across life support, farming, radio, and radiation shielding, then face an event: a solar flare, dust storm, meteor strike, equipment failure, or a calm day. On Mars, asking Earth for advice takes real minutes based on the actual current Earth-Mars distance (computed from JPL orbital elements), so players often must decide before help arrives, just like real astronauts.

How it works: A deterministic, seeded simulation engine (mulberry32 PRNG) generates each day’s events from a mission code, so the same code always replays the same mission. Radiation dose is computed from real reference values (Mars 0.67 mSv/day from Curiosity’s RAD instrument, Moon 1.37 mSv/day from Chang’e 4, ISS 0.73 mSv/day) combined with a shielding formula built from in-game choices (soil walls, shelter, shield cells), capped against NASA’s 600 mSv career radiation limit (NASA-STD-3001).

Benefits: Kids learn real orbital mechanics, radiation science, and resource trade-offs through play, not lecture. A built-in “Real-world check” after every storm shows exactly how much radiation was blocked versus an unshielded crew, using the real flare’s actual class.

Intended impact: Give younger students an intuitive, hands-on first encounter with space science and engineering trade-offs, encouraging interest in STEM and space careers.

Tools used: Vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (no frameworks, so it runs offline with zero install), a Python build script to assemble the single-file app, Node.js for the automated test suite (~72,800 checks), and Playwright for end-to-end browser testing across live, offline, and mobile conditions.

Creativity: Six selectable visual themes, animated base scenes, a built-in rule-based chat and voice guide (ARIA) that explains mechanics without needing any account or API key, a Shield Lab sandbox for experimenting with real flares, and non-punitive replayability so failure becomes a learning loop rather than a dead end.

Factors considered: Age-appropriateness (7–12), honesty about live vs. archived data, accessibility (keyboard navigation, screen-reader support, reduced-motion mode), and NASA Space Apps’ own guideline that no external account or API key should be required to use the tool.
